steps.body:
Every axis-aligned conic hides in the **general second-degree form**:

Ax² + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0.

You can name the conic just from the two squared coefficients **A and C** — before doing any algebra. The linear terms only shift it around; A and C set its shape.

widget.prompt: If A = C (equal, same sign), as in x² + y² − 6x + 4y + 9 = 0, the conic is a:

options.label: circle
options.feedback: Right — equal x² and y² coefficients give a circle.

options.label: parabola
options.feedback: A parabola needs ONE squared term missing. Equal A = C is a circle.

options.label: hyperbola
options.feedback: Hyperbolas need OPPOSITE signs. Equal A = C is a circle.

explanationVariants: x² + 4y² − 2x − 15 = 0 has A = 1, C = 4: same sign but unequal → an ellipse.
Both positive but A ≠ C means an ellipse (a stretched circle).

options.label: ellipse
options.feedback: Right — same sign, unequal coefficients: an ellipse.

options.label: circle
options.feedback: A circle needs A = C. Here 1 ≠ 4, so it's an ellipse.

options.label: hyperbola
options.feedback: Both coefficients are POSITIVE (same sign) → ellipse, not hyperbola.

steps.body: The two telltale signs: **opposite signs** on A and C mean a **hyperbola** (one term is subtracted); **exactly one squared term missing** (A = 0 or C = 0) means a **parabola** (only one variable is squared). These two rules complete the classification.

explanationVariants: 9x² − 4y² − 36 = 0 has A = 9, C = −4: opposite signs → a hyperbola.
The minus in front of y² (C < 0) is the hyperbola signal.

options.label: hyperbola
options.feedback: Right — opposite signs on A and C give a hyperbola.

options.label: ellipse
options.feedback: Ellipses need SAME signs. Opposite signs (9 and −4) → hyperbola.

options.label: circle
options.feedback: Opposite signs can't be a circle; this is a hyperbola.

explanationVariants: y² − 8x = 0 has C = 1 but A = 0 (no x² term) → a parabola.
Only ONE variable is squared, so it's a parabola.

options.label: parabola
options.feedback: Right — exactly one squared term means a parabola.

options.label: ellipse
options.feedback: An ellipse needs BOTH x² and y². With only y², it's a parabola.

options.label: hyperbola
options.feedback: A hyperbola also needs both squared terms. One squared term → parabola.

explanationVariants: 3x² + 3y² − 12 = 0 has A = C = 3 (equal, same sign) → a circle.
Equal coefficients on x² and y² always give a circle.
hints: Look only at the x² and y² coefficients.

options.label: circle
options.feedback: Right — A = C = 3, so it's a circle (of radius 2, once simplified).

options.label: ellipse
options.feedback: Equal coefficients (3 = 3) make a circle, not an ellipse.

options.label: parabola
options.feedback: Both terms are present and equal → circle.

takeaways: General form: Ax² + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0.
A = C → circle; same sign, A ≠ C → ellipse.
Opposite signs → hyperbola; one squared term missing → parabola.
steps.teaser: Next: completing the square to reach standard form.

concept.body: Classify from A, C in Ax²+Cy²+…: A=C → circle; same sign & A≠C → ellipse; opposite signs → hyperbola; one squared term missing → parabola.

explanationVariants: x² − y² − 1 = 0: A = 1, C = −1, opposite signs → hyperbola.

options.label: hyperbola
options.feedback: Right — opposite signs on A and C: a hyperbola.

options.label: circle
options.feedback: Opposite signs can't be a circle. It's a hyperbola.

options.label: ellipse
options.feedback: Ellipses need same signs; opposite signs → hyperbola.
